items.stem: The window in our classroom ____ by a football yesterday.

explain.why: 'broke' is active, but the window did not do the breaking; the football did, so a passive form is needed.
'yesterday' is a finished past time, so the present 'is broken' does not fit.
'The window' is singular, so 'were broken' does not agree with it.

solution: The window in our classroom was broken by a football yesterday.
The window receives the action and 'yesterday' is past, so use the simple past passive 'was broken' (singular subject).

items.stem: English ____ in all Singapore schools.

explain.why: 'English' is a singular subject, so 'are taught' does not agree.
'teaches' is active, but English does not teach anyone; it is the subject being taught, so the passive is needed.
'is teaching' is active, but English is not the one doing the teaching.

solution: English is taught in all Singapore schools.
English receives the action and the sentence states a general fact, so use the simple present passive 'is taught'.

items.stem: The new MRT station ____ by the Prime Minister last week.

explain.why: 'opened' is active, so it cannot be followed by 'by the Prime Minister' naming the doer.
'last week' is past time, so the present 'is opened' does not fit.
'has opened' is active and also clashes with 'last week'; the station was opened by someone.

solution: The new MRT station was opened by the Prime Minister last week.
'by the Prime Minister' names the doer of the action and 'last week' is past, so use the simple past passive 'was opened'.

items.stem: These cookies ____ by my grandmother every Chinese New Year.

explain.why: 'These cookies' is plural, so 'is baked' does not agree.
'baked' is active, so it cannot take 'by my grandmother' as the doer.
'are baking' is active, so it cannot take 'by my grandmother' as the doer.

solution: These cookies are baked by my grandmother every Chinese New Year.
The cookies receive the action and 'every Chinese New Year' shows a habit, so use the simple present passive 'are baked' (plural subject).

items.stem: The library books must ____ back by Friday.

explain.why: after 'must', 'return' is active, but the books do not return themselves; they are returned by pupils.
after the modal 'must' the verb must start with the base form, so 'returned' alone is wrong.
after the modal 'must' the passive needs 'be', not 'being'.

solution: The library books must be returned back by Friday.
A modal such as 'must' is followed by 'be' + past participle in the passive: 'must be returned'.

items.stem: A new playground ____ in our estate next month.

explain.why: 'will build' is active, but a playground cannot build itself; it is built by workers.
'will be building' is active continuous, but the playground is not doing the building.
'next month' is future, so the present perfect passive 'has been built' does not fit.

solution: A new playground will be built in our estate next month.
The playground receives the action and 'next month' is future, so use the future passive 'will be built'.

items.stem: My bicycle ____ from the void deck, so I reported it to the police.

explain.why: 'stole' is active, but the bicycle did not steal anything; it was taken from the owner.
'was stealing' is active, and the bicycle is not the thief.
'had stolen' is active, so it would mean the bicycle was the thief.

solution: My bicycle was stolen from the void deck, so I reported it to the police.
The bicycle receives the action of stealing, so use the simple past passive 'was stolen'.

items.stem: Rice ____ by farmers in many parts of Asia.

explain.why: 'grows' is active, so it cannot be followed by 'by farmers' naming the doer.
'grew' is active (and past), so it cannot take 'by farmers' as the doer.
'Rice' is an uncountable, singular subject, so 'are grown' does not agree.

solution: Rice is grown by farmers in many parts of Asia.
'by farmers' names the doer, so the verb is passive; 'Rice' is singular, so 'is grown'.

items.stem: The principal ____ the new library at the assembly yesterday morning.

explain.why: 'yesterday morning' is past, so the simple present 'opens' does not fit.
'was opened' is passive and cannot be followed by the object 'the new library'; the principal did the opening.
'has been opened' is passive and cannot take the object 'the new library'.

solution: The principal opened the new library at the assembly yesterday morning.
The subject 'The principal' does the action and the object 'the new library' follows, so the verb is active; 'yesterday morning' needs the simple past 'opened'.

items.stem: The school fair ____ every year in November.

explain.why: 'holds' is active, but the fair does not hold anything here; people hold the fair.
'is holding' is active, and the fair is not doing the holding.
'hold' is a plural active form, but 'The school fair' is singular and receives the action.

solution: The school fair is held every year in November.
The fair receives the action and 'every year' shows a regular event, so use the simple present passive 'is held'.

items.stem: Don't go in! The floor ____ at the moment.

explain.why: 'at the moment' shows the action is in progress, but 'is mopped' is the simple present passive for habits or facts.
'at the moment' means now, so the past 'was mopped' does not fit.
'has been mopping' is active, but the floor does not do the mopping.

solution: Don't go in! The floor is being mopped at the moment.
An action in progress now, done to the floor, takes the present continuous passive 'is being mopped'.

items.stem: Our school's new science lab ____ since June.

explain.why: 'since June' links the past to now, so the simple present 'is used' does not fit.
'since June' covers a period up to now, so the simple past 'was used' does not fit.
'has been using' is active, but the lab does not use anything; it is used by pupils.

solution: Our school's new science lab has been used since June.
'since June' needs the present perfect, and the lab receives the action, so use the present perfect passive 'has been used'.

items.stem: Ten new members ____ for the school choir so far.

explain.why: 'Ten new members' is plural, so 'has been chosen' does not agree.
'have been choosing' is active, but the members are the ones being chosen.
'so far' links the past to now, so the simple past 'were chosen' does not fit.

solution: Ten new members have been chosen for the school choir so far.
'so far' needs the present perfect and the members receive the action, so use 'have been chosen' (plural subject).

items.stem: The litter must ____ before the principal's visit tomorrow.

explain.why: 'clear' is active, but the litter cannot clear itself; it is cleared by someone.
'have cleared' is active, and the litter is not the one doing the clearing.
'be clearing' is active continuous, but the litter does not do the clearing.

solution: The litter must be cleared before the principal's visit tomorrow.
After the modal 'must', the passive is 'be' + past participle: 'must be cleared'.

items.stem: Several cars ____ in the car park last night, but nobody knows who did it.

explain.why: 'damaged' is active and would need an object after it, but none follows; the cars received the damage.
'have damaged' is active and clashes with 'last night'; the cars were the ones harmed.
'were damaging' is active, but the cars did not do the damaging.

solution: Several cars were damaged in the car park last night, but nobody knows who did it.
The cars receive the action and the doer is unknown, so use the agentless simple past passive 'were damaged'.

items.stem: The results ____ at the end of the week.

explain.why: 'will announce' is active, but results cannot announce anything; they are announced by the school.
'have announced' is active and past-linked, but 'at the end of the week' is future.
'will be announcing' is active continuous, but the results are not the ones announcing.

solution: The results will be announced at the end of the week.
The results receive the action and the time is future, so use the future passive 'will be announced'.

items.stem: The cleaners ____ the floor when the bell rang.

explain.why: 'were mopped' is passive and cannot take the object 'the floor'; the cleaners did the mopping.
'was mopped' is passive and does not agree with the plural 'cleaners'.
'had been mopped' is passive and cannot take the object 'the floor'.

solution: The cleaners were mopping the floor when the bell rang.
The cleaners do the action and 'the floor' is the object, so the verb is active; an action in progress when the bell rang takes the past continuous 'were mopping'.

items.stem: By the time we arrived, all the tickets ____.

explain.why: 'By the time we arrived' is in the past, so the present perfect 'have been sold' does not fit.
'all the tickets' is plural, so 'was sold' does not agree.
'we arrived' is past, so the future perfect 'will have been sold' does not fit.

solution: By the time we arrived, all the tickets had been sold.
'By the time we arrived' (past) needs the past perfect for an earlier action; the tickets receive the action, so 'had been sold'.

items.stem: The suspect ____ by the police at Changi Airport yesterday.

explain.why: 'arrested' is active, but 'by the police' names the doer, so the suspect must be the receiver.
'yesterday' is a finished time, so the present perfect passive does not fit.
'was arresting' is active, but the suspect did not do the arresting.

solution: The suspect was arrested by the police at Changi Airport yesterday.
'by the police' names the doer and 'yesterday' is past, so use the simple past passive 'was arrested'.

items.stem: Tickets for the school concert ____ online from tomorrow.

explain.why: 'can buy' is active, but tickets cannot buy anything; people buy them.
'can be buying' is active continuous, and tickets are not doing the buying.
'can have bought' is active and past-looking, but 'from tomorrow' is future.

solution: Tickets for the school concert can be bought online from tomorrow.
After the modal 'can', the passive is 'be' + past participle: 'can be bought'.

items.stem: The old school hall needs ____ before the concert.

explain.why: 'to repair' is active, but the hall does not repair anything; it receives the repair.
'to be repairing' is active continuous, but the hall is not doing the repairing.
'to have repaired' is active perfect, and it does not make the hall the receiver of the repair.

solution: The old school hall needs to be repaired before the concert.
The hall receives the action, so the passive infinitive 'to be repaired' follows 'needs'.

items.stem: The new cafeteria is said ____ by a famous chef.

explain.why: 'to have designed' is active, but 'by a famous chef' names the designer, so the cafeteria receives the action.
'to be designing' is active, but the cafeteria did not do the designing.
'to have been designing' is active continuous, but the cafeteria is not the designer.

solution: The new cafeteria is said to have been designed by a famous chef.
The design was done earlier and the cafeteria receives it, so use the perfect passive infinitive 'to have been designed'.

items.stem: Mum had the broken tap ____ by a plumber yesterday.

explain.why: in 'had + object + base form' the object does the action, but the tap does not fix itself; 'by a plumber' needs the past participle.
'fixing' would mean the tap was doing the fixing; the tap receives the action.
'had' + object is followed by the base form or a past participle, not by 'to fix'.

solution: Mum had the broken tap fixed by a plumber yesterday.
'have + object + past participle' means someone else does the action to the object: 'had the tap fixed'.

items.stem: Mei Ling was delighted about ____ the lead role by the drama teacher.

explain.why: 'giving' is active, which would make Mei Ling the giver; 'by the drama teacher' shows she received the role.
'having given' is active, which would make Mei Ling the giver.
'about' is a preposition here, so the verb takes an -ing form, and 'to give' is also active.

solution: Mei Ling was delighted about being given the lead role by the drama teacher.
After the preposition 'about' use an -ing form, and Mei Ling receives the role, so the passive gerund 'being given'.

items.stem: Nobody enjoys ____ by the teacher in front of the whole class.

explain.why: 'enjoy' is followed by an -ing form, not a to-infinitive.
'scolding' is active, but 'by the teacher' shows the person is the one scolded.
'enjoy' does not take a to-infinitive, and 'to scold' is active.

solution: Nobody enjoys being scolded by the teacher in front of the whole class.
'enjoy' is followed by an -ing form, and the person receives the scolding, so the passive gerund 'being scolded'.

items.stem: The temple is believed ____ over 200 years ago.

explain.why: 'over 200 years ago' refers to a time before now, so the present infinitive 'to be built' does not fit.
'to have built' is active, but a temple does not build itself.
'to have been building' is active continuous, but the temple is not the builder.

solution: The temple is believed to have been built over 200 years ago.
An earlier event that the temple receives needs the perfect passive infinitive 'to have been built'.

items.stem: The school ____ that the concert has been cancelled.

explain.why: 'has been announced' is passive and cannot be followed by the object clause 'that the concert has been cancelled'; the school is the one announcing.
'is announced' is passive and cannot take the 'that' clause as its object.
'was announced' is passive and cannot take the 'that' clause as its object.

solution: The school has announced that the concert has been cancelled.
The school does the announcing and 'that the concert has been cancelled' is the object, so the verb is active: 'has announced'.

items.stem: By 2030, many more HDB flats ____ in Punggol.

explain.why: 'will have built' is active, but flats do not build themselves.
'would have been built' refers to an unreal past, but 'By 2030' is a real future deadline.
'By 2030' is in the future, so the past perfect 'had been built' does not fit.

solution: By 2030, many more HDB flats will have been built in Punggol.
'By 2030' (a future deadline) takes the future perfect, and the flats receive the action, so 'will have been built'.

items.stem: If the road ____ earlier, the accident would not have happened.

explain.why: 'had repaired' is active, but a road does not repair itself.
the 'if' clause cannot contain 'would'; it takes the past perfect.
'would not have happened' signals an unreal past, so the 'if' clause needs the past perfect, not the present perfect.

solution: If the road had been repaired earlier, the accident would not have happened.
A past unreal condition uses 'if' + past perfect, and the road receives the action, so 'had been repaired'.

items.stem: I am looking forward to ____ to the Science Olympiad.

explain.why: 'to' is a preposition in 'look forward to', so it takes an -ing form, not the base form.
'inviting' is active and would need an object; here the speaker is the one who receives the invitation.
'having invited' is active and past-looking, but the speaker looks forward to receiving an invitation.

solution: I am looking forward to being invited to the Science Olympiad.
'look forward to' takes an -ing form because 'to' is a preposition, and the speaker receives the invitation, so 'being invited'.

items.stem:
Yesterday, Daniel said, "I am too tired to play." (He is fine today.)
Yesterday, Daniel said that he ____ too tired to play.

explain.why: he spoke yesterday and is fine today, so the reported verb is shifted back; 'is' would put the tiredness in the present.
'he' is singular, so 'were' does not agree.
he described how he felt then, not a future state, so 'will be' is wrong.

solution: Yesterday, Daniel said that he was too tired to play.
The state is over and the report is about the past, so 'am' shifts back to 'was'.

items.stem:
Last Monday, Alicia said, "I will visit my grandma tomorrow."
Last Monday, Alicia said that she would visit her grandma ____.

explain.why: 'tomorrow' would point to the day after the reporter speaks; the report is about the day after last Monday.
'yesterday' points backwards, but the visit was planned for the day after she spoke.
'the day before' points backwards, but the visit was planned for the day after she spoke.

solution: Last Monday, Alicia said that she would visit her grandma the next day.
In reported speech about a past occasion, 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day' (or 'the following day').

items.stem:
Mei Ling said, "My brother will fetch me."
Mei Ling said that ____ brother would fetch her.

explain.why: 'my' would refer to the person reporting, but the brother belongs to Mei Ling.
Mei Ling is a girl, so her own brother is 'her brother', not 'his brother'.
Mei Ling is one person, so the plural 'their' does not fit.

solution: Mei Ling said that her brother would fetch her.
'my' (the speaker's) becomes 'her' when we report what Mei Ling said.

items.stem:
Mrs Tan asked Kai, "Where do you live?"
Mrs Tan asked Kai where ____.

explain.why: a reported question keeps statement order, so the question form 'did he live' is wrong.
a reported question keeps statement order, so the question form 'does he live' is wrong.
the subject 'he' must come before the verb in a reported question.

solution: Mrs Tan asked Kai where he lived.
A reported question uses statement word order (subject + verb) with the tense shifted back: 'where he lived'.

items.stem:
"Please sit down," the teacher said to us.
The teacher ____ us to sit down.

explain.why: 'say' is not followed by a person and a to-infinitive; the pattern 'told us to sit' is needed.
'speak' is not used with a person object plus a to-infinitive.
'talk' is not used with a person object plus a to-infinitive.

solution: The teacher told us to sit down.
'tell + person + to-infinitive' reports an instruction; 'say' cannot take that pattern.

items.stem:
Last Tuesday, Jun Hao said, "I have finished my homework."
Last Tuesday, Jun Hao said that he ____ his homework.

explain.why: the report is about last Tuesday, so the present perfect shifts back to the past perfect.
'would finish' looks forward, but he said the homework was already finished.
'was finished his homework' is ungrammatical; the past perfect 'had finished' is needed.

solution: Last Tuesday, Jun Hao said that he had finished his homework.
In reported speech, the present perfect 'have finished' shifts back to the past perfect 'had finished'.

items.stem:
Yesterday, the driver said, "The bus will arrive soon." (It arrived five minutes later.)
Yesterday, the driver said that the bus ____ soon.

explain.why: the driver spoke yesterday and the bus has already arrived, so 'will' is shifted back to 'would'.
'arrived' says the arrival had happened, but he spoke before the bus came.
'would have arrived' is an unreal past, but the bus really did arrive later.

solution: Yesterday, the driver said that the bus would arrive soon.
In reported speech about a past occasion, 'will' shifts back to 'would'.

items.stem:
Last year, Priya said, "I can't swim." (She has learnt since then.)
Last year, Priya said that she ____ swim.

explain.why: she has learnt to swim since then, so 'can't' would still be reported as true; the report shifts back.
'wouldn't' is the shift of 'won't', not 'can't'.
'may not' changes the meaning from lack of ability to possibility.

solution: Last year, Priya said that she couldn't swim.
In reported speech, 'can't' shifts back to 'couldn't'.

items.stem:
"Do you want some water?" Aunty asked me.
Aunty asked me ____ I wanted some water.

explain.why: 'that' introduces a reported statement, not a yes/no question.
a reported question does not use 'do' as a link word; the joining word is 'if' or 'whether'.
'what' asks for a thing, but the original question could be answered yes or no.

solution: Aunty asked me if I wanted some water.
A yes/no question is reported with 'if' (or 'whether') and statement word order.

items.stem:
"Don't run along the corridor," the prefect told us.
The prefect told us ____ along the corridor.

explain.why: a reported command uses the to-infinitive; 'don't run' keeps the original direct form.
after 'told us' the verb needs 'to', so 'not run' is incomplete.
'didn't run' is a past statement, not a reported command.

solution: The prefect told us not to run along the corridor.
A negative command is reported as 'told + person + not to + verb'.

items.stem:
Yesterday, Mr Lim asked Aisha, "Did you finish the project?"
Yesterday, Mr Lim asked Aisha ____ the project.

explain.why: a reported question uses statement order, so 'had she' is wrong.
the direct-question form 'did she finish' is not used in a reported question; it also lacks a link word.
the question was asked yesterday about an earlier event, so the verb shifts back to the past perfect.

solution: Yesterday, Mr Lim asked Aisha if she had finished the project.
A reported yes/no question takes 'if' + statement order, and the past simple shifts back to the past perfect.

items.stem:
On Monday, Zara said, "I have a test today."
On Monday, Zara said that she had a test ____.

explain.why: 'today' would mean the day of the report, not Monday.
'the day before' points to a day earlier than Monday, but 'today' was Monday itself.
'the next day' points to the day after Monday, but 'today' was Monday itself.

solution: On Monday, Zara said that she had a test that day.
In reported speech about a past occasion, 'today' becomes 'that day'.

items.stem:
On Friday, Mum said, "I bought these mooncakes yesterday."
On Friday, Mum said that she ____ those mooncakes the day before.

explain.why: the report is about a Friday statement, so the past simple shifts back to the past perfect, not the present perfect.
'was buying' would mean the buying was in progress, but she said the buying was finished.
'would buy' looks forward, but 'the day before' is earlier.

solution: On Friday, Mum said that she had bought those mooncakes the day before.
'yesterday' becomes 'the day before' and the past simple 'bought' shifts back to 'had bought'.

items.stem:
Last week, the residents asked, "When will the lift be repaired?" (It was repaired the next day.)
The residents asked when the lift ____.

explain.why: the repair has already happened and the question was asked last week, so 'will' is shifted back to 'would'.
'would repair' is active, but the lift receives the repair.
'had been repaired' says the repair was already done, but the question was about a future time.

solution: The residents asked when the lift would be repaired.
'will be repaired' shifts back to 'would be repaired' in a reported question.

items.stem:
"I'm sorry I broke your pencil box," said Jia Wei to Ken.
Jia Wei ____ for breaking Ken's pencil box.

explain.why: 'suggested' does not fit 'for breaking'; Jia Wei was saying sorry, not offering an idea.
'complained' needs 'about', and Jia Wei was saying sorry, not blaming anyone.
'refused' takes a to-infinitive and contradicts the apology.

solution: Jia Wei apologised for breaking Ken's pencil box.
'I'm sorry' is reported with 'apologised for + -ing'.

items.stem:
"Let's have a picnic at East Coast Park," said Wei Xin.
Wei Xin ____ having a picnic at East Coast Park.

explain.why: 'promised' takes a to-infinitive, not '-ing', and 'Let's' is an idea, not a promise.
'complained' needs 'about', and 'Let's' is an idea, not a complaint.
'insisted' needs 'on' before 'having', and 'Let's' is a gentle idea, not a demand.

solution: Wei Xin suggested having a picnic at East Coast Park.
'Let's ...' is reported with 'suggested + -ing'.

items.stem:
Last year, Siti said, "I was late because the bus broke down."
Siti said that she was late because the bus ____ down.

explain.why: the report is about last year, so the past simple shifts back to the past perfect.
'would break' looks forward, but the breakdown was the reason for being late, so it came earlier.
'will break' is future, but the breakdown had already happened.

solution: Siti said that she was late because the bus had broken down.
The earlier action 'broke down' shifts back to the past perfect 'had broken down'.

items.stem:
"Shall I carry your bag?" Daniel asked Mrs Lee.
Daniel ____ to carry Mrs Lee's bag.

explain.why: 'Shall I ...?' is a polite offer, not a demand.
'refused to carry' would mean he would not carry it, which is the opposite of the offer.
'reminded' needs a person object before 'to', so 'reminded to carry' is incomplete.

solution: Daniel offered to carry Mrs Lee's bag.
'Shall I ...?' offering help is reported with 'offered to + verb'.

items.stem:
"I will help you," Jun Wei said to me.
Jun Wei ____ me that he would help.

explain.why: 'said' cannot take a person directly; it would need 'said to me'.
'spoke' is not followed by a person and a 'that' clause.
'explained' needs 'to me', so 'explained me that' is wrong.

solution: Jun Wei told me that he would help.
'tell' takes a person object directly before a 'that' clause.

items.stem:
Last year, Mr Goh said, "I have lived here for ten years."
Last year, Mr Goh said that he ____ there for ten years.

explain.why: the report is about last year's statement, so the present perfect shifts back to the past perfect.
'will live' is future, but he was counting years already lived.
'would have lived' is an unreal past, not a report of a real fact.

solution: Last year, Mr Goh said that he had lived there for ten years.
The present perfect 'have lived' shifts back to 'had lived'.

items.stem:
That evening, the usher asked us, "How long have you been waiting?"
The usher asked us how long we ____.

explain.why: the question was asked in the past, so the present perfect continuous shifts back to the past perfect continuous.
'would be waiting' looks forward, but the usher asked about waiting already done.
a reported question uses statement order, so 'had we been waiting' is wrong.

solution: That evening, the usher asked us how long we had been waiting.
The present perfect continuous shifts back to the past perfect continuous, in statement order.

items.stem:
Last month, Mr Yap said to Dev, "If I find your wallet, I will call you."
Mr Yap told Dev that if he ____ his wallet, he would call him.

explain.why: the report is about last month and 'would call' is shifted, so the 'if' verb must shift to the past too.
an 'if' clause does not take 'will' here; the verb shifts to the past.
an 'if' clause does not contain 'would'; the verb shifts to the simple past.

solution: Mr Yap told Dev that if he found his wallet, he would call him.
In a reported 'if' sentence, 'find' shifts to 'found' and 'will' shifts to 'would'.

items.stem:
"Give me your ticket," said Mr Lau, the conductor, to Raj.
Mr Lau told Raj to give ____ his ticket.

explain.why: 'me' referred to Mr Lau when he spoke; the reporter is a different person, so 'me' is wrong.
'you' referred to Raj when spoken; in a report about Raj, this becomes 'him', and the receiver of the ticket is Mr Lau.
Mr Lau is one person, so the plural 'them' does not fit.

solution: Mr Lau told Raj to give him his ticket.
'me' (Mr Lau speaking) becomes 'him' in the report.

items.stem:
"I didn't take your eraser," said Hui Min.
Hui Min denied ____ the eraser.

explain.why: 'deny' is followed by an -ing form, not a to-infinitive.
'deny' is followed by an -ing form, so the bare 'take' is wrong.
'took' is the simple past; after 'having' the past participle 'taken' is needed.

solution: Hui Min denied taking the eraser.
'deny' is followed by an -ing form.

items.stem:
"You copied my answers!" Ming said to Jo.
Ming ____ Jo of copying his answers.

explain.why: 'blame' is followed by 'for', not 'of'.
'criticise' is followed by 'for', not 'of'.
'warned' does not fit; Ming was charging Jo with something already done, not warning about a danger.

solution: Ming accused Jo of copying his answers.
'accuse someone of + -ing' reports a charge of wrongdoing.

items.stem:
"You should see a doctor," Mum said to me.
Mum advised me ____ a doctor.

explain.why: 'advise + person' is followed by a to-infinitive, not an -ing form.
'advise + person' needs 'to' before the verb.
'advised me should see' is ungrammatical; 'advise + person' needs a to-infinitive.

solution: Mum advised me to see a doctor.
'advise + person + to-infinitive' reports advice.

items.stem:
Vik said, "Had I known, I would have come."
Vik said that if he ____ known, he would have come.

explain.why: 'if he have known' is ungrammatical; the subject 'he' with a past perfect needs 'had'.
'if he has known' is a present perfect, which does not fit an unreal past condition.
'did known' is not a verb form; the past perfect 'had known' is needed.

solution: Vik said that if he had known, he would have come.
A past unreal condition keeps 'if + had + past participle' in reported speech.

items.stem:
Last Saturday, Su Lin asked Joel, "Are you coming to the party or not?"
Su Lin asked Joel whether ____ to the party or not.

explain.why: a reported question uses statement order, so 'was he coming' is wrong.
'he' is singular, so 'were' does not agree.
'he coming' has no finite verb after 'whether'.

solution: Su Lin asked Joel whether he was coming to the party or not.
'are coming' shifts back to 'was coming', in statement order after 'whether'.

items.stem:
"I'll definitely finish the model by Monday," Aaron said.
Aaron ____ to finish the model by Monday.

explain.why: 'admitted' means owning up to something done, not a plan for the future.
'denied' takes an -ing form and means saying 'no' to a claim.
'regretted' means feeling sorry, and does not fit a promise.

solution: Aaron promised to finish the model by Monday.
'I'll definitely ...' is a promise, reported with 'promised to + verb'.

items.stem:
"Don't forget to bring your passes," Mr Lee said to us.
Mr Lee ____ us to bring our passes.

explain.why: 'remembered' means recalling something himself; it does not take 'us to bring'.
'forgot' means he failed to remember, which is the opposite of what he said.
'recalled' means bringing something back to mind, and it does not take 'us to bring'.

solution: Mr Lee reminded us to bring our passes.
'Don't forget to ...' is reported with 'reminded + person + to-infinitive'.

items.stem: Kai swam in the pool, and so ____ his sister.

explain.why: 'swam' is past, so the matching auxiliary is 'did', not present 'does'.
'swam' is an ordinary verb, so the echo uses 'did', not a form of 'be'.
'swam' is the simple past, so the echo uses 'did', not 'had'.

solution: Kai swam in the pool, and so did his sister.
'so + auxiliary + subject' echoes the first clause; the simple past 'swam' is echoed by 'did'.

items.stem: "I can't speak Malay." "Neither ____ I."

explain.why: 'Neither' is already negative, so 'can't' makes a double negative.
'can't' is echoed with the same modal 'can', not 'do'.
'can't speak' is echoed with 'can', not with a form of 'be'.

solution: "I can't speak Malay." "Neither can I."
'Neither + auxiliary + subject' agrees with a negative statement; the auxiliary repeats the modal 'can'.

items.stem: My brother doesn't eat durian, nor ____ my father.

explain.why: 'my father' is singular, so 'do' does not agree; 'does' is needed.
'doesn't eat' is echoed with 'does', not a form of 'be'.
'doesn't eat' is present simple, so the echo is 'does', not 'will'.

solution: My brother doesn't eat durian, nor does my father.
'nor + auxiliary + subject' echoes a negative; 'doesn't' is echoed by 'does' with a singular subject.

items.stem: Not only ____ the first prize, but she also broke the school record.

explain.why: after 'Not only' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'she won' does not invert.
'she did' has the subject first, but after 'Not only' the auxiliary must come first.
inversion uses an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb 'won' alone.

solution: Not only did she win the first prize, but she also broke the school record.
A sentence starting with 'Not only' inverts: auxiliary + subject + base verb ('did she win').

items.stem: No sooner had we reached the bus stop ____ it began to rain.

explain.why: 'No sooner' is paired with 'than'; 'when' belongs with 'Hardly' or 'Scarcely'.
'then' is a time adverb and cannot link the two clauses here.
'that' does not complete 'No sooner'; the partner word is 'than'.

solution: No sooner had we reached the bus stop than it began to rain.
'No sooner' + past perfect is completed by 'than'.

items.stem: Hardly had I sat down ____ the bell rang.

explain.why: 'Hardly' is paired with 'when', not 'that'.
'then' is an adverb and cannot link the two clauses.
'while' means 'during the time that', but the bell rang right after sitting down; 'Hardly' is paired with 'when'.

solution: Hardly had I sat down when the bell rang.
'Hardly' + past perfect is completed by 'when'.

items.stem: Only after the guests left ____ the mess in the hall.

explain.why: after 'Only after ...', the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'we noticed' does not invert.
the subject 'we' is before the auxiliary, but 'Only after' needs 'did' first.
inversion needs an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb alone.

solution: Only after the guests left did we notice the mess in the hall.
A sentence starting with 'Only after ...' inverts: 'did we notice'.

items.stem: Never ____ such a delicious laksa before.

explain.why: after 'Never' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'I have eaten' does not invert.
after 'Never' at the start the sentence inverts, and 'before' needs the perfect form.
inversion uses an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb alone.

solution: Never have I eaten such a delicious laksa before.
A sentence starting with 'Never' inverts; 'before' with an experience takes the present perfect: 'have I eaten'.

items.stem: Amir is a punctual boy. Rarely ____ late for school.

explain.why: after 'Rarely' at the start, the verb comes before the subject; 'he is' does not invert.
'be' needs no 'do': 'does he late' has no main verb.
after 'Rarely' at the start the verb comes before the subject, so 'he was' is not inverted.

solution: Amir is a punctual boy. Rarely is he late for school.
A sentence starting with 'Rarely' inverts; with 'be' the verb simply moves before the subject: 'is he'.

items.stem: "I can ride a bike." "So ____ I."

explain.why: 'can ride' is echoed with the same modal 'can', not 'do'.
'can ride' is echoed with 'can', not with a form of 'be'.
'can ride' is echoed with 'can', not 'have'.

solution: "I can ride a bike." "So can I."
'So + auxiliary + subject' agrees with a positive statement; the auxiliary repeats the modal 'can'.

items.stem: Not only does the library lend books, ____ it also offers free workshops.

explain.why: 'Not only' is paired with 'but (also)', not 'so'.
'or' gives a choice, but the library does both things.
'then' is an adverb, and 'Not only' needs the conjunction 'but'.

solution: Not only does the library lend books, but it also offers free workshops.
'Not only ... but also ...' links two things done by the same subject.

items.stem: Hardly ____ the shop when the fire alarm rang.

explain.why: after 'Hardly' at the start, 'had' comes before the subject; 'we had' does not invert.
'Hardly ... when' uses the past perfect 'had entered', not 'did enter'.
the alarm rang in the past, so the past perfect 'had we entered' is needed, not 'have'.

solution: Hardly had we entered the shop when the fire alarm rang.
'Hardly' at the start inverts the past perfect: 'had + subject + past participle'.

items.stem: No sooner ____ off the lights than the baby started to cry.

explain.why: after 'No sooner' at the start, 'had' comes before the subject; 'I had' does not invert.
'No sooner ... than' uses the past perfect 'had switched', not 'did switch'.
the baby started to cry in the past, so the past perfect 'had I switched' is needed.

solution: No sooner had I switched off the lights than the baby started to cry.
'No sooner' at the start inverts the past perfect: 'had + subject + past participle'.

items.stem: Su Ling waited nervously. Only after the results were announced ____ how well she had done.

explain.why: after 'Only after ...' the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'she realised' does not invert.
inversion needs an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb alone.
the subject is before 'did', but 'Only after' needs 'did' first.

solution: Su Ling waited nervously. Only after the results were announced did she realise how well she had done.
'Only after ...' at the start inverts the main clause: 'did + subject + base verb'.

items.stem: Only when you finish your homework ____ allowed to play games.

explain.why: after 'Only when ...' the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'you will be' does not invert.
'are you allowed' is a present question form that misses the future meaning 'will'.
inversion needs the auxiliary 'will' before the subject, not a bare 'be'.

solution: Only when you finish your homework will you be allowed to play games.
'Only when ...' at the start inverts the main clause: 'will + subject + be'.

items.stem: "Alicia didn't go to the concert." "Neither ____ Wen Hui."

explain.why: 'didn't go' is past, so the echo uses 'did', not present 'does'.
'didn't go' is echoed with 'did', not a form of 'be'.
'Neither' is already negative, so 'didn't' makes a double negative.

solution: "Alicia didn't go to the concert." "Neither did Wen Hui."
'Neither + auxiliary + subject' echoes a negative; 'didn't go' is echoed by 'did'.

items.stem: Scarcely ____ the stage when the audience began to clap.

explain.why: after 'Scarcely' at the start, 'had' comes before the subject; 'she had' does not invert.
the audience clapped in the past, so the past perfect 'had she reached' is needed.
'Scarcely ... when' uses the past perfect 'had reached', not 'did reach'.

solution: Scarcely had she reached the stage when the audience began to clap.
'Scarcely' at the start inverts the past perfect: 'had + subject + past participle'.

items.stem: Not until the guests arrived ____ the cake.

explain.why: after 'Not until ...' the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'we cut' does not invert.
the subject is before 'did', but 'Not until' needs 'did' first.
inversion needs an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb alone.

solution: Not until the guests arrived did we cut the cake.
'Not until ...' at the start inverts the main clause: 'did + subject + base verb'.

items.stem: So heavy ____ that the match was cancelled.

explain.why: after 'So heavy' at the start, the verb comes before the subject; 'the rain was' does not invert.
'be' does not take 'do'; 'did the rain' has no main verb.
the match was cancelled in the past, so the past 'was the rain' is needed.

solution: So heavy was the rain that the match was cancelled.
'So + adjective' at the start inverts the verb 'be' before the subject: 'was the rain'.

items.stem: Seldom ____ such a large crowd at this hawker centre.

explain.why: after 'Seldom' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'we see' does not invert.
inversion needs an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb alone.
the subject is before 'do', but 'Seldom' needs 'do' first.

solution: Seldom do we see such a large crowd at this hawker centre.
'Seldom' at the start inverts the main clause: 'do + subject + base verb'.

items.stem: "I wasn't at the meeting." "Neither ____ I."

explain.why: 'wasn't' is a form of 'be', so the echo uses 'was', not 'did'.
'I' takes 'was', not 'were'.
'wasn't' is past, so the echo is 'was', not present 'am'.

solution: "I wasn't at the meeting." "Neither was I."
'Neither + auxiliary + subject' echoes a negative; 'wasn't' is echoed by 'was'.

items.stem: "Mum doesn't like spicy food." "Neither ____ Dad."

explain.why: 'Dad' is singular, so 'do' does not agree; 'does' is needed.
'Neither' is already negative, so 'doesn't' makes a double negative.
'doesn't like' is echoed with 'does', not a form of 'be'.

solution: "Mum doesn't like spicy food." "Neither does Dad."
'Neither + auxiliary + subject' echoes a negative; 'doesn't like' is echoed by 'does' with a singular subject.

items.stem: Not only the students but also the teacher ____ finished the project.

explain.why: with 'Not only ... but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the teacher', which is singular.
'is finished the project' is ungrammatical; the perfect needs 'has finished'.
'are finished the project' is ungrammatical; the perfect needs 'has finished'.

solution: Not only the students but also the teacher has finished the project.
With 'Not only ... but also ...' the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it: 'the teacher' takes 'has'.

items.stem: Only by practising every day ____ the violin well.

explain.why: after 'Only by ...' the modal comes before the subject; 'you can play' does not invert.
the subject must follow the modal, not come after the main verb.
'can' is already an auxiliary, so 'do' is not added.

solution: Only by practising every day can you play the violin well.
'Only by ...' at the start inverts the main clause: modal + subject + base verb.

items.stem: ____ I known about the road closure, I would have taken the MRT.

explain.why: 'Have I known' does not form an unreal past condition; the past perfect needs 'Had'.
'Did I known' is ungrammatical; 'Did' takes the base form.
'Would I known' is ungrammatical; 'would' needs a base verb.

solution: Had I known about the road closure, I would have taken the MRT.
'Had + subject + past participle' replaces 'If I had known' in a past unreal condition.

items.stem: "Siti has never been late." "Nor ____ Hui Min."

explain.why: 'has been' is a present perfect, so the echo uses 'has', not 'is'.
'has been' is echoed with 'has', not 'does'.
'Hui Min' is singular, so 'have' does not agree.

solution: "Siti has never been late." "Nor has Hui Min."
'Nor + auxiliary + subject' echoes a negative; 'has been' is echoed by 'has'.

items.stem: Not only did the volunteers clean the beach, but they ____ the old signboards.

explain.why: after 'did' in the first part, the second part needs a past verb 'repaired', not the base form.
'repairing' without 'were' is not a finite past verb.
'had repair' is not a verb form; the simple past 'repaired' is needed.

solution: Not only did the volunteers clean the beach, but they also repaired the old signboards.
In the 'but' part of 'Not only ... but also', the verb is in the normal order and in the same past tense: 'also repaired'.

items.stem: Only after the final bell had rung ____ the classroom.

explain.why: after 'Only after ...' the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'the pupils left' does not invert.
the subject is before 'did', but 'Only after' needs 'did' first.
the leaving came after the bell, so the main clause uses the simple past 'did ... leave', not the past perfect.

solution: Only after the final bell had rung did the pupils leave the classroom.
'Only after ...' at the start inverts the main clause: 'did + subject + base verb'.

items.stem: Ben missed the start of the briefing. Not only ____ late, but he also forgot his notes.

explain.why: after 'Not only' at the start the verb comes before the subject; 'he was' does not invert.
'be' does not take 'do'; 'did he late' has no main verb.
'did' is the wrong auxiliary for 'be', and the subject is also before it.

solution: Ben missed the start of the briefing. Not only was he late, but he also forgot his notes.
'Not only' at the start inverts 'be' before the subject: 'was he'.

items.stem: At no time during last term ____ the pupils allowed to use phones in class.

explain.why: 'the pupils' is plural, so 'was' does not agree.
'last term' is past, so 'are' does not fit.
'have the pupils allowed' needs 'been' to be passive.

solution: At no time during last term were the pupils allowed to use phones in class.
'At no time' at the start inverts: verb 'be' before the subject, here past and plural: 'were the pupils'.
